title: Statistics - Lesson 1: Reading Statistical Reports Assessment
description: Checkpoint assessment on reading statistical reports and judging evidence.

questions.question: Which set lists the main parts to check when reading a statistical report?
options: Claim, source, display, statistic, conclusion
Compass, ruler, protractor, triangle, circle
Theme, plot, speaker, stanza, rhyme
Variable, exponent, coefficient, radical, factor
questions.explanation: This lesson focuses on reading the claim, source, display, statistic, and conclusion together.

questions.question: A report says, "The average score rose from 21 to 26 points, so the review program helped." Which part is the statistic?
options: The average score rose from 21 to 26 points
The word "helped"
The title of the report
The reader's opinion
questions.explanation: The statistic is the numerical summary used as evidence: the average changed from 21 to 26.

questions.question: A survey asked 80 learners, and 52 chose practice quizzes. What percent chose practice quizzes? Enter the percent with the percent sign.
If a survey is voluntary, it may overrepresent people who feel strongly about the topic.
questions.explanation: Voluntary response can introduce bias because people with strong opinions may be more likely to respond.

questions.question: A graph has a title but no vertical-axis label. What is the best criticism?
options: The units or meaning of the values are unclear.
The title makes all values false.
The graph must be a circle graph.
The data source is automatically representative.
questions.explanation: Without an axis label, readers may not know whether the values are counts, percents, scores, pesos, or another unit.

questions.question: A school-wide claim is based on 18 responses from one club. Which conclusion is most careful?
options: The result may describe that club, but it is weak evidence for the whole school.
The result proves the school-wide claim.
The result is invalid because all surveys are invalid.
The result needs no source because it has a number.
questions.explanation: The sample is narrow, so a careful conclusion limits the claim and raises a representativeness concern.

questions.question: A report compares 42 learners in August with 45 learners in September. How many more learners attended in September? Enter just the number.
A cut-off vertical scale can make a small difference look large.
questions.explanation: When the scale starts near the data values instead of at zero, visual differences can appear exaggerated.

questions.question: Which sentence best uses evidence without exaggerating?
options: In the surveyed group, 60% preferred printed modules, so most surveyed learners preferred printed modules.
Everyone prefers printed modules because 60% of one survey did.
Printed modules are always the best because the bar is tallest.
No conclusion can ever be written from survey data.
questions.explanation: The sentence gives the statistic and limits the conclusion to the surveyed group.

questions.question: A report says "72% agreed" but gives no sample size or question. Name two pieces of information you need before judging the claim.
questions.correctAnswer: I need to know how many people were surveyed and what exact question they answered.
questions.explanation: The sample size and survey question are needed to understand what the 72% actually means.

questions.question: A table shows 24 learners prefer videos, 18 prefer printed modules, and 18 prefer group study. What claim is directly supported?
options: Videos were the most selected option in this table.
All learners prefer videos.
Printed modules and videos are equally preferred.
Group study was chosen by more learners than videos.
questions.explanation: Videos have the highest count, 24, so they were the most selected option in this table.

questions.question: In a table, 24 + 18 + 18 learners are counted. What is the total number of learners? Enter just the number.
Explain why a statistical conclusion should not describe a larger population unless the sample supports it.
questions.correctAnswer: A limited or biased sample may not represent the larger population, so the conclusion could exaggerate what the data show.
questions.explanation: Statistical conclusions should match the group actually measured unless the sample was selected to represent a larger population.

questions.question: Which question best helps evaluate the data source of a report?
options: Who was measured, how many were included, and how were they chosen?
Which font did the report use?
How long is the first paragraph?
Does the report have exactly four colors?
questions.explanation: The group, sample size, and selection method are central source details.

questions.question: Write a careful conclusion: A survey of 100 Grade 10 learners found that 58 prefer review videos.
questions.correctAnswer: The data show that 58 of 100 surveyed Grade 10 learners, or 58%, prefer review videos, so a claim that most surveyed learners prefer review videos is supported.
questions.explanation: The conclusion names the statistic, identifies the surveyed group, and states the level of support without overgeneralizing.
